claims.text: Adjusting the atomic content of constituent elements in HEAs can improve heat-transfer capability.
Adjusting the atomic content of constituent elements can preserve the structural integrity of HEAs.
Changing elemental atomic content produces changes in lattice distortion.
Changing elemental atomic content produces changes in atomic behavior.
Incorporating larger atoms into a lattice of smaller atoms causes lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch reduces lattice thermal conductivity.
Elemental atomic content can be adjusted to control the lattice thermal conductivity of an HEA.
The proposed intervention will improve performance relative to current intermediate-layer performance.
The predicted improvement should hold from 300 K to 1100 K.
The predicted behavior should hold for simulated HEA dimensions from 60 Å to 200 Å.
HEA size affects lattice thermal conductivity at the nanoscale.
The effects of composition, size, and temperature on HEA thermophysical properties are not fully understood.
Molecular dynamics can be used to evaluate lattice thermal conductivity and volumetric specific heat capacity in an HEA.
Measurements of lattice thermal conductivity and volumetric specific heat capacity are sufficient to determine whether structural integrity is preserved.

contradictions.description: The mechanism emphasizes that larger-atom-induced lattice distortion reduces lattice thermal conductivity, whereas the predicted outcome is improved heat-transfer capability. The hypothesis does not explain how reduced thermal conductivity yields improved heat transfer or specify an alternative composition change that increases conductivity.

The falsification rule requires preservation of structural integrity under loading, but no mechanical loading condition or structural-integrity measurement is specified; the proposed measurements cover only thermal conductivity and heat capacity.
